description: AeroReborn is an innovative team participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. Our mission is to explore creative and data-driven solutions to identify, analyze, and rethink the future of abandoned aircraft. By combining technology, innovation, and teamwork, we aim to transform forgotten aircraft into opportunities for a more sustainable and resourceful future.
summary: AeroReborn is a mobile-first web experience that tells the true stories of the machines humanity left on the Moon and Mars. Visitors choose a world, enter a hangar of 11 machines from 6 NASA missions (from Surveyor 3 and the Apollo 11 and 12 lunar modules to Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity and Ingenuity) and "wake up" each one. Each machine's life is told in acts computed from its own sourced dates: departure, planned mission, overtime, silence, and what remains today. 187 dated moments, illustrated with 283 real NASA pictures, are swiped like a short-video feed, with hard words explained, read-along narration and a quiz. Every fact is stored with its NASA source (402 sources in total) and the API refuses to start if a fact has none. Aimed at young people aged 10 to 15, AeroReborn turns open NASA archives (catalogues, image libraries, mission journals) into stories they can follow, and shows that every machine left more than a trace: it passed something on.
details:
AeroReborn is a free, public website that turns the machines left on the Moon and Mars into characters with a life story. The journey has three steps: choose a destination (the Moon or Mars, shown as rotating 3D globes), enter the hangar of that world (11 machines from 6 NASA missions: Surveyor 3, the Apollo 11 and Apollo 12 lunar module descent stages, the Apollo 11 EASEP and laser retroreflector, the Apollo 12 ALSEP, the Mars Pathfinder lander, Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity and Ingenuity), then open one machine to follow its whole life.

A machine's story is not a fixed template. Its acts are computed from its own sourced dates: departure, the planned mission, overtime (with the real ratio, e.g. Opportunity lived 57 times longer than its planned 90 Martian days), the silence after its last signal, and what remains today. Each act shows dated moments (187 in total) illustrated with real NASA pictures (283), which phone users swipe like a short-video feed. Hard words are explained in brackets and in a 45-word glossary, a read-along narration highlights the text as it is spoken, a short quiz closes each story with the fact behind every answer, and a "for us on Earth" section explains what each machine taught us.

Scientific rigour is built into the code: every fact shown is stored with the identifiers of its sources (402 NASA sources, each with its URL and date of access), and the content is validated when the API starts; an unsourced fact stops the server instead of being published. Facts, interpretations and imagination are kept apart, and any picture that is not a photograph (diagram, simulation, artist's view) carries a visible label. All pictures are real NASA material; none is AI-generated.

NASA's archives are open but hard to read for young people: scattered across catalogues, image libraries and mission journals, full of jargon and units. AeroReborn gives them a way in through stories, emotions (the silence of a machine that stopped answering) and facts they can check. It can be used at home or in class, on any phone, and is available in English, French and Wolof (interface). The intended impact is curiosity: understanding that each mission is a long effort, that machines often outlive their plans, and that what they sent back changed what we know.

TypeScript everywhere. Frontend: React 19, Vite, Tailwind CSS, React Router, three.js (3D globes), Google model-viewer (3D models from NASA 3D Resources), the Web Audio API (soundtrack synthesised in the browser). Backend: Node.js and Express, serving the validated JSON content as an API. Hosting: Vercel (static site, the API as a serverless function, NASA pictures resized on the fly about 5 times lighter). Quality: Vitest and Testing Library, oxlint, GitHub Actions. Code: https://github.com/biramth/aeroreborn

Each machine's narrative structure comes from its data rather than a script; the story starts from its last signal, then rewinds to its launch; the photo feed borrows the gestures of short-video apps to keep young readers scrolling through real science; the visual direction ("Transmission") presents the site as signals received from far away.

Accuracy (nothing invented, every fact sourced, AI-drafted texts marked as drafts until expert review), honesty about images (photos versus diagrams or artist's views), accessibility (native buttons and links, visible focus, keyboard and screen readers, reduced motion respected, touch targets of at least 44 px), phones first (pictures resized, a light graphics mode so older iPhones stay stable), languages, and independence (no NASA logo or branding; the site states it is not affiliated with or endorsed by NASA).
